{{about|graphs embedded in the plane, with crossings|graph embeddings on other surfaces|topological graph theory}}
[[File:Oddpair.jpg|thumb|upright=1.35|A graph with odd-crossing number 13 and pair-crossing number 15<ref name=PSS08 />]]
In [[mathematics]], a '''topological graph''' is a representation of a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] in the [[Euclidean plane|plane]], where the [[vertex (graph theory)|''vertices'']] of the graph are represented by distinct points and the [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|''edges'']] by [[Jordan arc]]s (connected pieces of [[Jordan curve|''Jordan curves'']]) joining the corresponding pairs of points. The points representing the vertices of a graph and the arcs representing its edges are called the ''vertices'' and the ''edges'' of the topological graph. 
It is usually assumed that any two edges of a topological graph cross a finite number of times, no edge passes through a vertex different from its endpoints, and no two edges touch each other (without crossing). A topological graph is also called a ''drawing'' of a graph.

An important special class of topological graphs is the class of ''geometric graphs'', where
the edges are represented by ''line segments''. (The term ''[[geometric graph]]'' is sometimes used in a broader, somewhat vague sense.)

The theory of topological graphs is an area of [[graph theory]], mainly concerned with [[combinatorics|combinatorial]] properties of topological graphs, in particular, with the crossing patterns of their edges. It is closely related to [[graph drawing]], a field which is more application oriented, and [[topological graph theory]], which focuses on embeddings of graphs in surfaces (that is, drawings without crossings).

== Extremal problems for topological graphs ==

A fundamental problem in [[extremal graph theory]] is the following: what is the maximum number of edges that a graph of ''n'' vertices can have if it contains no subgraph belonging to a given class of ''forbidden subgraphs''? The prototype of such results is [[Turán's theorem]], where there is one forbidden subgraph: a [[complete graph]] with ''k'' vertices (''k'' is fixed). Analogous questions can be raised for topological and geometric graphs, with the difference
that now certain ''geometric subconfigurations'' are forbidden.

Historically, the first instance of such a theorem is due to [[Paul Erdős]], who extended
a result of [[Heinz Hopf]] and [[Erika Pannwitz]].<ref name=HP34>{{Citation|last1=Hopf|first1=Heinz|author1-link=Heinz Hopf |last2=Pannwitz|first2=Erika|author2-link=Erika Pannwitz| year=1934 |title=Aufgabe nr. 167|journal=Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung |volume=43|page=114}}</ref> He proved that the maximum number of edges that a geometric graph with ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;2 vertices can have without containing ''two disjoint edges'' (that cannot even share an endpoint) is ''n''. [[John Horton Conway|John Conway]] conjectured that this statement can be generalized to simple topological graphs. A topological graph is called "simple" if any pair of its edges share at most one point, which is either an endpoint or a common interior point at which the two edges properly cross. Conway's [[thrackle]] conjecture can now be reformulated as follows: A simple topological graph with ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;2 vertices and no two disjoint edges has at most ''n'' edges.

The first linear upper bound on the number of edges of such a graph was established by [[László Lovász|Lovász]] et al.<ref name=LPS96>{{Citation |last2=Pach|first2=János |author2-link=János Pach|last1=Lovász|first1=László|author1-link=László Lovász|first3=Mario|last3=Szegedy|author3-link=Mario Szegedy|title=On Conway's thrackle conjecture |journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]]| publisher = Springer| year =1997|volume=18|issue=4|pages=369–376|doi=10.1007/PL00009322|doi-access=free}}</ref>
The best known upper bound, 1.3984''n'', was proved by Fulek and [[János Pach|Pach]].<ref name=FP19>{{citation
| last1 = Fulek | first1 = Radoslav
 | last2 = Pach | first2 = János | author2-link = János Pach
 | arxiv = 1708.08037
 | doi = 10.1016/j.dam.2018.12.025
 | journal = [[Discrete Applied Mathematics]]
 | pages = 226–231
 | title = Thrackles: An improved upper bound
 | volume = 259
 | year = 2019 }}.</ref> Apart from geometric graphs, Conway's thrackle conjecture is known to be true for ''x''-monotone topological graphs.<ref name="PS11">{{citation
 | last1 = Pach | first1 = János | author1-link = János Pach
 | last2 = Sterling | first2 = Ethan

 | title = Conway's conjecture for monotone thrackles
 | volume = 118
 | year = 2011| s2cid = 17558559}}</ref> A topological graph is said to be ''x-monotone'' if every vertical line intersects every edge in at most one point.

[[Noga Alon|Alon]] and [[Paul Erdős|Erdős]]<ref name="AE89">{{citation|

vertices, containing no 3 disjoint edges is ''O''(''n''). The optimal bound of roughly 2.5''n'' was determined by Černý.<ref name="C05">{{citation|

For the number of edges in a simple topological graph with no ''k'' disjoint edges, only an <math>O(n\log^{4k-8} n)</math> upper bound is known.<ref name=PT03>{{citation |last2=Tóth|first2=Géza|last1=Pach|first1=János|author1-link=János Pach|contribution=Disjoint edges in topological graphs |title=Combinatorial Geometry and Graph Theory: Indonesia-Japan Joint Conference, IJCCGGT 2003, Bandung, Indonesia, September 13-16, 2003, Revised Selected Papers|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|publisher=Springer-Verlag|volume=3330| year =2003|pages=133–140|doi=10.1007/978-3-540-30540-8_15|isbn=978-3-540-24401-1 |url=http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/129363/files/disjointreprint.pdf}}</ref> This implies that every complete simple topological graph with ''n'' vertices has at least <math>c\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}</math> pairwise disjoint edges, which was improved to <math>cn^{\frac 12-\epsilon}</math> by Ruiz-Vargas.<ref>{{citation

=== Quasi-planar graphs ===

A common interior point of two edges, at which the first edge passes from one side of the second edge to the other, is called a ''crossing''. Two edges of a topological graph ''cross'' each other if they determine a crossing. For any integer ''k''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1, a topological or geometric graph is called  ''k-quasi-planar'' if it has no ''k'' pairwise crossing edges.
Using this terminology, if a topological graph is 2-quasi-planar, then it is a ''planar graph''.
It follows from [[Euler's polyhedral formula]] that every [[planar graph]] with ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;2 vertices has at most 3''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;6 edges.  Therefore, every 2-quasi-planar graph with ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;2 vertices has at most 3''n''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;6 edges.

It has been conjectured by Pach et al.<ref name=PSS96>{{Citation |last1=Pach|first1=János |author1-link=János Pach|last2=Shahrokhi|first2=Farhad|first3=Mario|last3=Szegedy|title=Applications of the crossing number |journal=[[Algorithmica]]| publisher = Springer| year =1996|volume=16|issue=1|pages=111–117|doi=10.1007/BF02086610|s2cid=20375896 }}</ref> that every ''k''-quasi-planar topological graph with ''n'' vertices has at most ''c''(''k'')''n''
edges, where ''c''(''k'') is a constant depending only on ''k''. This conjecture is known to be true for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3
<ref name=AAPPS97>{{citation

== Crossing numbers ==
{{main|Crossing number (graph theory)}}
Ever since [[Pál Turán]] coined [[Turán's brick factory problem|his ''brick factory problem'']]
<ref name=T77>{{citation |last1=Turán|first1=Paul|title=A note of welcome |journal=[[Journal of Graph Theory]]|year =1977|volume=1|pages=7–9 |doi=10.1002/jgt.3190010105}}</ref> during [[World War II]], the determination or estimation of [[Crossing number (graph theory)|crossing numbers of graphs]] has been a popular theme in graph theory and in the theory of algorithms<ref>{{citation|author=[[Michael Garey|Garey, M. R.]]; [[David S. Johnson|Johnson, D. S.]] |title=Crossing number is NP-complete |journal=SIAM Journal on Algebraic and Discrete Methods |volume=4 |pages=312–316 |year=1983 |mr=0711340 |doi=10.1137/0604033 |issue=3 }}</ref> that is abundant with famous long standing open problems such as the [[Albertson conjecture]], [[Crossing number (graph theory)#Complete graphs and graph coloring|Harary-Hill's conjecture]]<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Balogh | first1 = József 
 | last2 = Lidický | first2 = Bernard 
 | last3 = Salazar | first3 = Gelasio 
 | arxiv = 1711.08958
 | doi = 10.1137/17M1158859
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics]]
 | pages = 1261–1276
 | title = Closing in on Hill's conjecture
 | volume = 33
 | number = 3
 | year = 2019 | s2cid = 119672893 
 }}</ref> or the still unsolved [[Turán's brick factory problem]].<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Schaefer | first1 = Marcus 
 | journal = [[Electronic Journal of Combinatorics]]
 | pages = DS21–May
 | title = The graph crossing number and its variants: A survey
 | doi = 10.37236/2713
 | year = 2012| volume = 1000 
 | article-number = DS21: Dec 22 
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref> However, the publications in the subject (explicitly or implicitly) used several competing definitions of crossing numbers. This was pointed out by Pach and Tóth,<ref name=PT00/> who introduced the following terminology.

[[crossing number (graph theory)|Crossing number]] (of a graph ''G''): The minimum number of crossing points over all drawings of ''G'' in the plane (that is, all of its representations as a topological graph) with the property that no three edges pass through the same point. It is denoted by cr(''G'').

''Pair-crossing number'': The minimum number of crossing pairs of edges over all drawings of ''G''. It is denoted by pair-cr(''G'').

''Odd-crossing number'': The minimum number of those pairs of edges that cross an odd number of times, over all drawings of ''G''. It is denoted by odd-cr(''G'').

These parameters are not unrelated. One has odd-cr(''G'')&nbsp;≤&nbsp;pair-cr(''G'')&nbsp;≤&nbsp;cr(''G'') for every graph ''G''. It is known that cr(''G'')&nbsp;≤&nbsp;2(odd-cr(''G''))<sup>2</sup><ref name=PT00>{{citation |last2=Tóth|first2=Géza|last1=Pach|first1=János|title=Which crossing number is it anyway?|journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series = Series B | year =2000|number=2|volume=80|pages=225–246|doi=10.1006/jctb.2000.1978|doi-access=free}}</ref> and <math>O(\operatorname{pcr}(G)^{\frac{3}{2}}\log^{2}\operatorname{pcr}(G))</math><ref name=M13>{{Citation |last1=Matoušek|first1=Jiří |contribution=Near-optimal separators in string graphs|title=Combin. Probab. Comput.|volume=23|number=1| pages =135–139 | year =2014| doi=10.1017/S0963548313000400 |arxiv=1302.6482|s2cid=2351522 }}</ref>
and that there exist infinitely many graphs for which pair-cr(''G'')&nbsp;≠&nbsp;odd-cr(''G'').<ref name=PSS08>{{citation  |last1=Pelsmajer |first1=Michael J.|last2=Schaefer|first2=Marcus  |last3=Štefankovič |first3=Daniel |year=2008  |title=Odd crossing number and crossing number are not the same |journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]] |volume=39 |issue=1–3 |pages=442–454 |doi=10.1007/s00454-008-9058-x |doi-access=free }} A preliminary version of these results was reviewed in {{citation |title= Proc. of 13th International Symposium on Graph Drawing| year=2005 |pages= 386–396 |doi=10.1007/11618058_35|doi-access=free}}</ref>
<ref name=G08>{{citation  |last1=Tóth |first1=Géza | year=2008  |title=Note on the pair-crossing number and the odd-crossing number |journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]] |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=791–799 |doi=10.1007/s00454-007-9024-z|doi-access=free }}.</ref> No examples are known for which the crossing number and the pair-crossing number are not the same. It follows from the [[Hanani–Tutte theorem]]<ref name=C34>{{citation
|first1=Chaim (Haim)|last1=Chojnacki (Hanani)
|title= Uber wesentlich unplattbar Kurven im dreidimensionale Raume
|journal =Fundamenta Mathematicae
|volume = 23
|year=1934
|pages=135–142|doi=10.4064/fm-23-1-135-142
|doi-access=free
}}
</ref>
<ref name=T70>{{citation
|first1=William T.|last1=Tutte
|title= Toward a theory of crossing numbers
|journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]
|volume = 8
|year=1970
|pages=45–53
|doi=10.1016/s0021-9800(70)80007-2|doi-access=
}}
</ref> that odd-cr(''G'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 implies cr(''G'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.
It is also known that odd-cr(''G'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''k'' implies ''cr(G)=k'' for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1,&nbsp;2,&nbsp;3.<ref>{{citation  |last1=Pelsmajer |first1=Michael J.|last2=Schaefer|first2=Marcus  |last3=Štefankovič |first3=Daniel |year=2007|title=Removing even crossings  |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series = Series B |volume=97 |issue=4 |pages=489–500 |doi=10.1016/j.jctb.2006.08.001 |doi-access= }}
</ref>
Another well researched graph parameter is the following.

''Rectilinear crossing number'': The minimum number of crossing points over all straight-line drawings of ''G'' in the plane (that is, all of its representations as a geometric graph) with the property that no three edges pass through the same point. It is denoted by lin-cr(''G'').

By definition, one has cr(''G'')&nbsp;≤&nbsp;lin-cr(''G'') for every graph ''G''. It was shown by Bienstock and Dean that there are graphs with crossing number 4 and with arbitrarily large rectilinear crossing number.<ref name=BD93>{{citation  |last1=Bienstock|first1=Daniel|last2=Dean|first2=Nathaniel|title=Bounds for rectilinear crossing numbers  |journal=[[Journal of Graph Theory]] |volume=17 |year=1993|issue=3|pages=333–348|doi=10.1002/jgt.3190170308}}
</ref>

Computing the crossing number is [[NP-completeness|NP-complete]]<ref name=gj>{{cite journal |author1=Garey, M. R. |author-link=Michael Garey |author2=Johnson, D. S. |author2-link=David S. Johnson |title=Crossing number is NP-complete |journal=SIAM Journal on Algebraic and Discrete Methods |volume=4 |pages=312–316 |year=1983 |mr=0711340 |doi=10.1137/0604033 |issue=3 }}</ref> in general. Therefore a large body of research focuses on its estimates. The [[Crossing number inequality|Crossing Lemma]] is a cornerstone result that provides widely applicable lower bounds on the crossing number. Several interesting variants and generalizations of the Crossing Lemma are known for Jordan curves<ref name=FPT18>{{citation
 | last1 = Pach | first1 = János | author1-link = János Pach
 | last2 = Rubin | first2 = Natan 
 | last3 = Tardos | first3 = Gábor | author3-link = Gábor Tardos
 | arxiv = 1708.02077
 | doi = 10.1016/j.aim.2018.03.015 | doi-access = free
 | journal = [[Advances in Mathematics]]
 | pages = 908–940
 | title = A crossing lemma for Jordan curves
 | volume = 331
 | year = 2018 | s2cid = 22278629 }}</ref>
<ref name=PT19>{{citation
 | last1 = Pach | first1 = János | author1-link = János Pach
 | last2 = Tóth | first2 = Géza 
 | arxiv = 1706.06829
 | doi = 10.1016/j.jctb.2018.12.002
 | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series = Series B
 | pages =  104–111
 | title = Many touchings force many crossings
 | volume = 137
 | year = 2019 }}</ref> and degenerate crossing number,<ref name=AP13>{{citation
 | last1 = Ackerman| first1 = Eyal
 | last2 = Pinchasi  | first2 = Rom
 | doi = 10.1007/s00454-013-9493-1
 | journal = [[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]
 | pages =  695–702
 | title = On the Degenerate Crossing Number
 | volume = 49
 | year = 2013| issue = 3
 | s2cid = 254030772
 }}</ref><ref name=SS15+>{{citation
 | last1 = Schaefer | first1 = Marcus 
 | last2 = Štefankovič | first2 = Daniel 
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-27261-0_6
 | contribution=The degenerate crossing number and higher-genus embeddings
 | title = Graph Drawing: 23rd International Symposium, GD 2015, Los Angeles, CA, USA, September 24-26, 2015, Revised Selected Papers
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science 
 | pages =  63–74
 | year = 2015| volume = 9411 
 | doi-access = free 
 | isbn = 978-3-319-27260-3 
 }}</ref> where the latter relates the notion of the crossing number to the [[Graph embedding|graph genus]].

== Ramsey-type problems for geometric graphs ==

In traditional [[graph theory]], a typical [[Ramsey theory|Ramsey-type result]] states that if we color the edges of a sufficiently large complete graph with a fixed number of colors, then we necessarily find a ''monochromatic'' subgraph of a certain type.<ref name=GRS90>{{Citation  |publisher= Wiley|first1=Ronald L.|last1=Graham|author-link=Ronald Graham|last2=Rothschild|first2=Bruce L.|first3=Joel H.|last3=Spencer|author-link3=Joel Spencer|year=1990|title=Ramsey Theory}}</ref> One can raise similar questions for geometric (or topological) graphs, except that now we look for monochromatic (one-colored) substructures satisfying certain geometric conditions.<ref name=K13>{{citation  |last1=Károlyi|first1=Gyula|contribution=Ramsey-type problems for geometric graphs |title=Thirty essays on geometric graph theory|editor-first=J.|editor-last=Pach|editor-link=János Pach| publisher = Springer| year =2013 }}</ref>
One of the first results of this kind states that every complete geometric graph whose edges are colored with two colors contains a non-crossing monochromatic ''[[spanning tree]]''.<ref name=KTP97>{{Citation |last1=Károlyi |first1=Gyula J.|last2=Pach |first2=János|last3=Tóth|first3=Géza |year=1997  |title=Ramsey-type results for geometric graphs, I |journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]] | issue=3 |volume=18 |pages=247–255 |doi=10.1007/PL00009317|doi-access=free }}</ref> It is also true that every such geometric graph contains <math>\left\lceil \frac{n+1}{3} \right\rceil</math> disjoint edges of the same color.<ref name=KTP97 /> The existence of a non-crossing monochromatic path of size at least ''cn'', where ''c''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0 is a constant, is a long-standing [[open problem]]. It is only known that every complete geometric graph on ''n'' vertices contains a non-crossing monochromatic path of length at least <math>n^{\frac 23}</math>.<ref name=KTPV98>{{Citation |last1=Károlyi |first1=Gyula J.|last2=Pach |first2=János|last3=Tóth|first3=Géza |first4=Pavel|last4=Valtr|year=1998  |title=Ramsey-type results for geometric graphs, II |journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]] | issue=3 |volume=20 |pages=375–388 |doi=10.1007/PL00009391|doi-access=free }}
</ref>

== Topological hypergraphs ==

If we view a topological graph as a topological realization of a 1-dimensional ''[[simplicial complex]]'', it is natural to ask how the above extremal and Ramsey-type problems generalize to topological realizations of ''d''-dimensional simplicial complexes. 
There are some initial results in this direction, but it requires further research to identify the key notions and problems.<ref>{{Citation  |
    first =János|last=Pach|author-link=János Pach
  | contribution =  Geometric graph theory |title= Handbook of Discrete and Computational Geometry|edition=2nd|series=Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications|editor1-link=Jacob E. Goodman|editor1-last=Goodman|editor1-first= Jacob E.|editor2-link=Joseph O'Rourke (professor)|editor2-last=O'Rourke|editor2-first= Joseph
  | year = 2004
  | publisher = Chapman and Hall/CRC}}
</ref><ref name=MTW09>
{{Citation |last1=Matoušek|first1=Jiří |author1-link=Jiří Matoušek (mathematician)|last2=Tancer|first2=Martin |last3=Wagner|first3=Uli|year=2009|contribution=Hardness of embedding simplicial complexes in <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math>|title=Proceedings of the Twentieth Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms |pages=855–864}}
</ref><ref name=B04>
{{Citation |last1=Brass|first1=Peter| year=2004|contribution=Turán-type problems for convex geometric hypergraphs|title=Towards a Theory of Geometric Graphs|editor-first= J.|editor-last= Pach|editor-link=János Pach|series=Contemporary Mathematics|publisher=American Mathematical Society|pages=25–33}}
</ref>

Two vertex disjoint simplices are said to ''cross'' if their relative interiors have a point in common. A set of ''k''&nbsp;>&nbsp;3 simplices ''strongly cross'' if no 2 of them share a vertex, but their relative interiors have a point common.

It is known that a set of ''d''-dimensional simplices spanned by ''n'' points in <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math> without a pair of crossing simplices can have at most <math>O(n^{d})</math> simplices and this bound is asymptotically tight.<ref name=DP98>
{{Citation |last1=Dey |first1=Tamal K.|author1-link=Tamal Dey|last2=Pach |first2=János |year=1998 |title=Extremal problems for geometric hypergraphs |journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]] | issue=4 |volume=19|pages=473–484 |doi=10.1007/PL00009365|doi-access=free }}</ref> This result was generalized to sets of 2-dimensional simplices in <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math> without three strongly crossing simplices.<ref name="S11+">{{Citation|contribution=A note on geometric 3-hypergraphs |last1=Suk|first1=Andrew|year=2013|title=Thirty Essays on Geometric Graph Theory|editor-first= J.|editor-last=Pach|editor-link=János Pach| publisher=Springer}} arXiv:1010.5716v3</ref>
If we forbid ''k'' strongly crossing simplices, the corresponding best known upper bound is <math>O(n^{d+1-\delta})</math>,<ref name=DP98 /> for some <math>
\delta =\delta (k,d)<1 </math>. This result follows from the colored [[Tverberg theorem]].<ref name=VZ92>
{{Citation|title=The colored Tverberg's problem and complexes of injective functions |last1=Živaljević|first1=Rade T.|first2=Siniša T.|last2=Vrećica|year=1992|journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series = Series A| doi=10.1016/0097-3165(92)90028-S|volume=61|issue=2|pages=309–318|doi-access=free}}
</ref> It is far from the conjectured bound of <math>O(n^{d})</math>.<ref name=DP98 />

For any fixed ''k''&nbsp;>&nbsp;1, we can select at most <math>O(n^{\lceil \frac{d}{2} \rceil})</math> ''d''-dimensional simplices spanned by a set of ''n'' points in <math>\mathbb{R}^d</math> with the property that no ''k'' of them share a common interior point.<ref name=DP98 /><ref name=BF87>
{{Citation |last1=Bárány|first1=Imre| first2=Zoltán |last2=Fürédi |year=1987 |title=Empty simplices in Euclidean-space |journal=[[Canadian Mathematical Bulletin]] | issue=4 |volume=30|pages=436–445 |doi=10.4153/cmb-1987-064-1|hdl=1813/8573 |s2cid=122255929 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> This is asymptotically tight.

Two triangles in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> are said to be ''almost disjoint'' if they are disjoint or if they share only one vertex.  It is an old problem of [[Gil Kalai]] and others to decide whether the largest number of almost disjoint triangles that can be chosen on some vertex set of ''n'' points in <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> is  <math>o(n^2)</math>. It is known that there exists sets of ''n'' points for which this number is at least <math>cn^{\frac 32}</math> for a suitable constant ''c''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Károlyi|first1=Gyula| last2=Solymosi |first2=József|author2-link= József Solymosi |year=2002 |title=Almost disjoint triangles in 3-space|journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]] | issue=4 |volume=28|pages=577–583|doi=10.1007/s00454-002-2888-z|doi-access=free}}
</ref>
